1. Implementation

The document has been created and approved by the General Assembly of 09.11.2024.
The document and its rules have been implemented since the 2025 season.

2. Definition

“Greaves” is the term used to describe all lower leg protections.
Types of Greaves:

● 1-Panel Greaves (Half-Greaves)

Made of 1 plate of metal forged to the shape of the lower leg.
Attached by a leather strap at the back of the calf.

● 2-Panel Greaves (Cased Greaves)

Made of 2 plates of metal built to protect the lower leg at 360°.
The plates are built with hinges and attached by a leather strap at the inner side of the lower leg.

● 3-Panel Greaves
Made of 3 plates of metal attached with leather.

● 3/4 Greaves

The front side of the lower leg is protected by a metal plate.
The outside of the lower leg is protected by a half-plate of metal, leaving the inner side of the lower
leg unprotected.

● Splinted Greaves

Metal plates riveted to a leather base.
The plates are alternately outside and inside the leather.

● Brigand Greaves

Metal plates riveted to a fabric base.
The plates are covered by the fabric.

● Eastern Greaves

Due to very few historical sources, it is allowed to use eastern stylization of European Greaves.
Allowed designs are displayed in the document “Eastern Armors.”

3. General Requirements

Historical Basis: Must be based on historical sources.
Anatomical Shape: Must have the anatomical shape of the lower leg.
Proportions: Must reproduce the proportions based on historical sources.

Malleolus Protection: Must protect the malleolus bone.

4. One Panel Greaves (Half-Greaves)

4.1. Historical Sources and Datation

The 1-panel greave is the earliest form of lower leg protection available for knights, originating in the
early 14th century.

They are Approved for 14th century and Transitional armors.

They are Denied for 15th century armors.

4.2. Historical References

Crucifixion, Niederhaslach — 1360, France J. von Falkenstein — 1365, Germany

4.3. Specific Requirements for One Panel Greaves (Half-Greaves)

They must follow the General Requirements (see Section 3 above).
The entire front of the lower leg must be covered by the greaves.

5. Two Panels Greaves (cased greaves)

5.1. Historical Sources and Datation

2-panel greaves, also known as cased greaves, were the most common form of lower leg protection
from 1370 to 1600 and later. They provided superior protection for competitors by covering the entire
lower leg from all sides.

They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.

Metropolitan Museum of Arts - 1450 Brescia - 1470/1480 - Italy

5.2. Specific Requirements

They must follow the General Requirements (see Section 3 above).
2-panel greaves are Approved if worn with the adequate armor style from the 15th century.
2-panel greaves at the bottom or top of the greaves are Denied for 15th century armor.

6. Three Panels Greaves

6.1. Historical Sources and Datation

3-panel Greaves are mainly represented in Germany from 1360 to 1380. They consist of one front panel
and two side panels, articulated by leather straps.

They are Approved for 14th century and Transitional armors.

They are Denied for 15th century armors.

6.2. Historical Example

Sir Burchard von Steinberg — 1376, Germany

6.3. Specific Requirements

They must conform to the General Requirements (see Section 3 above).
The side panels must protect both sides of the lower leg, including the malleolus bone.
The panels can be articulated with leather straps or a piece of leather between each panel.

It is Allowed to extend the width of the side panels to cover the back of the calf, despite this not being
based on historical proportions.

It is Allowed to use hinges instead of leather despite it not being documented by historical sources.

8. Splinted Greaves

8.1. Historical Sources and Datation

Splinted Greaves are represented in Europe from 1350 to 1380. They consist of metal plates riveted to a
leather base.

They are Approved for 14th century and Transitional armor.
They are Denied for 15th century armor.

8.2. Historical Examples

IIS A\\iEP

Louis Thys — 1365, Belgium G. von Schwarzburg — 1349, Germany

8.3. Specific Requirements for Splinted Greaves

They must conform to the General Requirements (see Section 3 above).

They must be made of metal plates with the following features:
● rectangular shape,
● firmly riveted to a leather base,
● plates must be riveted alternatively inside and outside the leather base,
● plates must conform to the anatomical shape of the lower leg.

9. Brigand Greaves

9.1. Historical Sources and Datation

Brigand Greaves are represented in Europe from 1350 to 1380. They consist of metal plates riveted to a
fabric base.

They are Approved for 14th century and Transitional armors.

They are Denied for 15th century armors.

9.2. Specific Requirements for Brigand Greaves

They must conform to the General Requirements (see Section 3 above).
They must be made of metal plates with the following features:

● rectangular shape,

● firmly riveted to a leather base,

● plates must be riveted inside the fabric, not outside,

● plates must conform to the anatomical shape of the lower leg.
